explainers.title: Hello and welcome to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This subject is a little bit different from your other lessons. It is not about learning lots of facts by heart. Instead, it helps you grow thinking skills that you will use all your life.

There are six thinking skills in Global Perspectives. You will grow all of them, year by year:

This whole unit is about the first skill: Research. It is a lovely skill to start with, because you need it before all the others. You cannot look closely at a topic until you have found out about it first.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful way.
Analysis — looking closely at a topic and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how good an idea or a fact really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn.
Collaboration — working well with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas so others understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You learn in the Ehel Academy way. Three kinds of help work together:

In the old way of this subject, children were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'talk as a class'. In our way, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, have a real chat with it. Say your ideas out loud or type them.

Your research skills will grow in three steps this year, like a young tree. First you are starting a skill. Then you are developing it. Then you are getting better at it. Do not worry if a skill feels tricky at first. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.
bullets: You, at your own speed. You read, think and do the activities in your own time. You can go slowly on a hard part, or quickly on an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. When this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor like a friendly helper. It will chat about your ideas and answer your questions at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work and ask big questions.

explainers.title: Meet Sana, our researcher for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 4 learner all the way through. Her name is Sana, and she is a pupil at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

One day at school, Sana looks around at break time. Some children run and play. Some sit and look at a phone. Some look tired. Sana starts to wonder: how do the children at my school keep fit and healthy, and how could more of them be active?

That question becomes Sana's research project for this unit. As you meet each new skill, you will see what Sana does with it. By the end, she will have real answers to share with her teacher. You will do the very same thing, with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds one big project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a topic that matters in the wider world and also right where you live. You come back to it, lesson after lesson. Each new skill adds another piece.

Sana's Challenge is about keeping fit and healthy. Here are some good Challenge topics for Year 4. Any of these could be yours:

Your classmates will care about different things. Layla wants more children to join in sport. Karim wonders where the rice and dates in the market come from. Nadia thinks children today sit too much. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge.

You do not have to choose right now. As you work, keep a note of any topic that makes you curious. That curious feeling is a great sign of a good Challenge topic.
bullets: How children keep fit and healthy, and how to help more of them be active
How children spend their time after school, and screen-time on phones and computers
Where our food comes from, and which foods grow near us or come from far away
How children live in other countries, and how they are the same as or different from us

explainers.title: So what is research?
explainers.body:
Many people think research just means typing a question into a phone. Real research is more careful than that. Research means finding out about a topic or a question in an organised way, so you can trust what you learn and share it with others.

When you research well, you do three things, and this unit teaches all three:

Let us try a small piece of research about food. It shows that research is part of everyday life.
bullets: Ask good questions about your topic.
Find useful sources to answer them, like books, websites, and people who know.
Keep a record of what you find, so it is clear and helpful.

explainers.title: Start a research book
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a simple habit that real researchers use. Keep a research book. This can be a notebook or a computer file where you write everything about your Challenge as you go. Each time you work, write the date, then what you did, what you found, and what you want to do next.

A research book helps you in three ways. It keeps your questions, sources and results in one place. It shows how your ideas change over time. And it makes sharing your findings much easier, because the work is already there. Keep your research book beside you as you read on.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Making your own questions
explainers.body:
Every piece of research starts with a question. A good question helps you find out what you really want to know. Many good questions start with one of these little words:

Try to make lots of questions first. You can choose the best ones later. More questions mean more to find out.
bullets: What ... happens? What do children do after school?
Where ... does it happen? Where do children play?
Why ... does it happen? Why do some children do little sport?
How ... does it happen? How can we help more children be active?

explainers.title: Skill 2: The steps of an investigation, in order
explainers.body:
When you find something out, we call it an investigation. An investigation works best in the right order. If you mix up the steps, it is much harder. Here are the six steps in order:

Notice that thinking of your questions comes early, and telling others comes last. You cannot share your results until you have collected them first.
bullets: Decide on a topic to find out about.
Think of questions to ask.
Make a questionnaire (a sheet of questions).
Ask some people your questions.
Record your results.
Tell others what you found out.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Making a questionnaire and asking people
explainers.body:
A questionnaire is a sheet of questions you ask lots of people. When you ask one person your questions, that is an interview. Questionnaires and interviews help you find out what many people do or think.

Sana wants to know how children spend their time after school. She makes a simple questionnaire like this, with a row for each activity and a place to write the hours:

Then Sana asks the same questions to a few children and writes down what they say. Now she has real information she can look at.
bullets: Homework — hours each week: ______
Sport or active play — hours each week: ______
Phone or computer — hours each week: ______
Jobs at home — hours each week: ______
Watching TV — hours each week: ______

explainers.title: Skill 4: Open questions and number questions
explainers.body:
There are two handy kinds of question. It helps to know both.

Both are useful. Number questions are easy to count and put in a chart. Open questions tell you more about why. Good research often uses some of each.
bullets: An open question lets people answer in their own words. For example: 'What do you like to do after school?' You get lots of detail.
A number question asks for a number. For example: 'How many days a week do you play sport?' You get answers you can count and add up.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Recording your results in a pictogram
explainers.body:
Once you have collected your answers, you need to record them so a pattern shows. A lovely way to do this is a pictogram. A pictogram is a picture chart. Each little picture, or icon, stands for one thing, such as one person.

Sana and her group asked 10 children how much time they spend on each activity each week. They drew one figure for each child. This is what they found:

A pictogram makes the pattern easy to see. In one look, Sana can tell that children do lots of homework, phone and TV, but very little sport. That gives her something important to think about.
bullets: Homework — most children spend more than 3 hours.
Sport or active play — most children spend less than 1 hour.
Phone or computer — most children spend more than 3 hours.
Watching TV — most children spend more than 3 hours.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Finding answers in a source
explainers.body:
A source is anywhere your information comes from: a book, a website, a video, or a person who knows. A clever trick is to pick the right source for your question. Different questions need different sources.

Look how well each question matches a source:

Here is a great habit. Before you read a source, write down the questions you hope it will answer. As you read, tick each question the source answers. If some questions are not answered, you know to look in another source.
bullets: How can I get better at a team sport? A short video that shows you how.
What foods make a healthy meal? A recipe magazine or a healthy-food website.
What fun things can I do outdoors? A children's website about outdoor games.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Using more than one source, and making notes
explainers.body:
One source is a good start, but it is even better to use more than one source. Different sources tell you different things. When they agree, you can trust the answer more.

When you read a source, you do not copy it. You make notes. Notes are short and in your own words. A neat way to keep notes tidy is to sort them under headings. A heading is a title for a group of notes.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Are children the same or different around the world?
explainers.body:
A big Global Perspectives question is this: are children around the world the same as you, or different? People have different answers, and each answer is a perspective. A perspective is a way of seeing something.

Some children think we are mostly the same everywhere. Others think there are big differences. To find out, Ehel Academy wrote to partner schools in other countries. Children there wrote back about how they spend their time.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Checking what the evidence really shows
explainers.body:
After you collect results, you can say what they show. But be careful. Only say what your evidence proves. Evidence is the facts you have gathered. A simple star rating helps you check a statement:

This keeps you honest. You do not say more than your results can prove.
bullets: Three stars — the evidence fully shows this is true.
Two stars — the evidence mostly shows this.
One star — the evidence might show this.
A cross — the evidence does not show this at all.

explainers.title: Skill 10: Asking an elder, and choosing the best questions
explainers.body:
Some of the best sources are the people around you, especially older family members. An elder, like a grandparent, has seen many changes. They can tell you how life was long ago.

When you interview an elder, the questions you choose really matter. Open questions get the richest answers.

explainers.title: Skill 11: Showing your findings with a chart or a poster
explainers.body:
Your findings are only useful if others can understand them. So you show them clearly. A chart, like a pictogram, is great for numbers. A poster is great for sharing a message and getting people to change.

Sana wants to help children be more active. Did you know that more than 8 in 10 young people around the world do not move around enough? Sana decides to make a poster to persuade children to be more active.

explainers.title: How research helps the other five skills
explainers.body:
Research is the first skill for a good reason. It helps all the others.

So the work you do now is never wasted. It is the ground the whole subject is built on.
bullets: Analysis needs good information before you can look closely at why things happen.
Evaluation needs facts before you can decide how good an idea is.
Reflection grows when you notice how your research changed your mind.
Collaboration works better when everyone brings well-researched ideas.
Communication is stronger when facts stand behind your message.

explainers.title: Putting it all together
explainers.body: You have now met every research skill in this unit. Here is the whole journey in simple steps:
bullets: Pick a topic and make good questions.
Choose sources and make a questionnaire.
Ask people, using open and number questions.
Record your results in a pictogram or chart.
Use more than one source, and make notes under headings.
Check what the evidence really shows.
Share your findings with a chart or a poster.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Analysis. Once you can research a topic well, analysis helps you look closely and ask why things happen. Strong research now makes strong analysis easy later. Well done for starting your Global Perspectives journey so well.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real topics, like the food we eat and how children keep fit.
But the real prize is to become a good researcher who can find out about almost anything.

bigIdeas.title: A quick way to remember
lines: Topic first. Questions next. Then a questionnaire.
Then ask people. Then record what they say.
Then share what you found. Six steps, always in order.

bigIdeas.title: How to draw a pictogram
lines: Choose a small picture to stand for one person, like a stick figure.
Draw one picture for each person who gave that answer.
Add a key that says: one picture means one child.
Give your pictogram a clear title so everyone knows what it shows.

bigIdeas.title: The same, and different, all at once
lines: Children everywhere play, learn, and eat with their families.
At festivals, some families share sweet treats at one celebration, others share a special meal at another, and others hold a feast after a good harvest.
The foods are different, but the joy of sharing is the same. A fair researcher notices both.

bigIdeas.title: Sana's Then and Now poster
lines: Title at the top: Keep moving, keep healthy!
A Then side: long ago, children walked and played outside a lot. That was good. But they had less sports kit. That was not so good.
A Now side: today, children have more sports at school. That is good. But many sit for a long time on phones. That is not so good.
The poster asks children to take the best from then and now: move more, and play outside.
A good poster is clear, has a big title, uses pictures, and gives one strong message. It should make someone want to do something different.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one topic that matters to you and to other people. This is your Challenge.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you really care about.
By the end you will have real research to share with your teacher.

bigIdeas.title: Why the order matters
lines: You cannot make a questionnaire until you have thought of your questions first.
You cannot record results until you have asked people.
Telling others always comes last, because you need something to tell them.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It is short and easy to understand.
It is about your topic.
It can be answered quickly.
It does not push people to one answer. Ask 'How much sport do you do?', not 'You love sport, do you not?'.

bigIdeas.title: Being a kind interviewer
lines: Say hello and thank the person for helping you.
Ask one question at a time, and listen carefully.
It is fine to ask them to say more about an answer you like.
Never rush them. A good interview feels like a friendly chat.

models.title: Where does my food come from?
lines: Sana looks at the food at home: bananas, a mango, rice, dates, and anjero for breakfast.
She asks a clear question: which of these foods grow near Hargeisa in the Horn of Africa, and which come from far away?
She finds out: some fruit grows close by, but the rice, the dates, and the flour for anjero often arrive by ship at Berbera port, then travel by truck to markets in Hargeisa and Mogadishu.
Now Sana knows something new about her food, just by asking and finding out. That is real research.
So research is not a strange, school-only thing. It is a careful, honest way to find things out, and you can get better and better at it.

models.title: Sana makes her questions
lines: Sana wants to help children be more active.
How much do children move around each day?
Why do some children do very little sport?
What could help children be more active after school?
Sana now has good questions to guide her research.

models.title: Sana asks two friends
lines: Sana interviews Leila and Omar with her questionnaire.
She asks each of them the same questions, so she can compare their answers fairly.
She writes their answers in her research book, one column for each friend.
Asking the same questions to everyone is what makes a questionnaire fair.

models.title: Turning an open question into a number question
lines: Open question: How do you spend your time after school?
Number question: How many hours a week do you spend on a phone or computer?
The open question gives a rich answer. The number question gives an answer you can count.
Sana asks both, so she gets the whole picture.

models.title: Sana reads a source about keeping fit
lines: Sana finds a source called How children can keep fit in a busy world.
Before reading, she writes three questions she hopes it answers.
As she reads, she ticks the two questions it answers, and leaves one unticked.
Now Sana knows exactly what she still needs to find somewhere else.

models.title: Sana makes notes under headings
lines: Sana is finding out how children kept fit long ago. She uses these headings:
Ways they were active: they walked a lot, and played outside games.
Keeping fit at school: they ran and played in the schoolyard.
Keeping fit at home: they helped with jobs and fetched things.
Sana keeps her notes short, in her own words, under each heading.
Sometimes a heading has no notes at all, and that is fine. It just means that source did not tell you about that part. You can look for it in your next source.

models.title: Letters from partner schools
lines: Grace, in Kenya, wrote: We play football at break, and I walk to school.
Rohan, in India, wrote: I do lots of homework, and I love cricket after school.
Amara, in Nigeria, wrote: I help at home, and we play games outside in the evening.
Sana compares their days with her own. Some things are the same, and some are different.
Comparing your life with children far away is a wonderful way to see many perspectives. It helps you notice that people can be different and still share a lot.

models.title: Sana rates two statements
lines: Sana's pictogram showed children do lots of homework and little sport.
Statement: children spend more time on homework than on sport. Sana gives it three stars, because her evidence clearly shows it.
Statement: children do not enjoy sport. Sana gives this a cross, because her results never asked about enjoying sport at all.
Sana only says what her evidence really shows.

models.title: Sana asks her grandmother
lines: A narrow question: Did you play outside? The answer is just yes.
An open question: How did children keep fit when you were young? Now Sana's grandmother tells a whole story.
She says: We walked everywhere, and we played games outside until dark.
The open question told Sana far more, so it was the better question.
Before an interview, it helps to make a mind map. Write your topic in the middle, then draw lines out to the things you want to ask about, such as games, school, and food long ago.

models.title: Sana's whole journey
lines: Sana turned a wonder about keeping fit into good questions.
She made a questionnaire and asked her friends.
She recorded the results in a pictogram, and saw children do little sport.
She used more than one source, and asked her grandmother about the past.
She checked her evidence with stars, then made a poster to help children be active.
You will do the very same thing with your own Challenge, one small step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Topic in the middle: keeping fit at my school.
Questions around it: What do children do at break? Why do some do little sport? How can we help more children be active? Where do children like to play?
These questions come from different angles, which is exactly what you want.

models.title: A model questionnaire
lines: Topic: how children keep fit.
Question 1: How many days a week do you play sport or run around?
Question 2: What is your favourite way to be active?
Question 3: How many hours a day do you spend sitting still?
Notice there are number questions and open questions mixed together.

models.title: A model pictogram
lines: Title: How my friends spend time after school.
Homework: four figures. Sport: two figures. Phone or computer: five figures.
Key: one figure means one child.
In one look, you can see which activity is the most popular.

models.title: A model poster plan
lines: Message: children should move more and play outside.
Title: Keep moving, keep healthy!
Pictures: children playing football, a child walking to school, a happy face.
One clear message, a big title, and pictures that help. That is a strong poster.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor. Tell it: I am starting Unit 1 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Research.
Ask it: In one or two simple sentences, why is research useful, even outside school?
Then say which of the six skills you think will be easiest for you, and which will be hardest.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you think research means now.
Ask it: Is my idea missing anything?
Then ask it to give you one everyday example of research that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one topic you care about.
Ask it to help you make four questions about it, using What, Where, Why and How.
Then ask: which of my questions is the most interesting to find out about?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the six steps of an investigation in the order you remember them.
Ask it to check that your order is right.
Ask it: which step do you think people forget the most, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor two things you would like to find out from other children.
Ask it to help you write three simple questionnaire questions.
Ask it: are my questions easy to understand and quick to answer?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your AI tutor one open question and one number question about your topic.
Ask it to check that each one is the right kind.
Ask it: when is a number question more useful than an open question?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what you would count in a pictogram about your topic.
Ask it what small picture would work well to stand for one person.
Ask it: what title should I give my pictogram so it is clear?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one question you have about your topic.
Ask it what kind of source would answer it best: a book, a website, a video, or a person.
Ask it to help you write two questions to look for before you read.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor two headings you could use for notes about your topic.
Ask it to check that your headings are clear.
Ask it: why is it better to use two sources than only one?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one way you think children everywhere are the same.
Ask it to help you think of one way children might be different in different places.
Ask it: what question could I ask a child in another country to find out more?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one thing your results seem to show.
Ask it to help you decide how many stars your evidence gives it.
Ask it: is there anything I am saying that my results do not really prove?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor who you could interview about the past.
Ask it to help you write three open questions for your interview.
Ask it: how can I make sure my questions are polite and kind?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the one message you want your poster to share.
Ask it to help you think of a short, catchy title.
Ask it: what one picture would make my message stronger?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your topic and your two reasons.
Ask it: is this a good size of topic for Year 4, or is it too big?
Ask it to help you make the topic more about where you live.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your number 1 choice and your reason.
Ask it which choice it would put first, and why.
Ask it: is there a healthy choice not on the list that you would add?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it which two questions look the most interesting, and why.
Ask it to suggest one good question you did not think of.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your order to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check that your six steps are in the right order.
Ask it to explain any step you put in the wrong place.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are any of my questions hard to understand, or do any push people to one answer?
Ask it to help you fix any question that is not quite right.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what your pictogram shows.
Ask it: what is the clearest thing my pictogram tells us?
Ask it if my title makes it easy to understand.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four pairs to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check your matches.
Ask it: for my own Challenge, which kind of source would help me most?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any you found tricky.
Ask it: when is a number question more useful than an open question?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three interview questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are my questions open, so they get long answers?
After the interview, tell it what you learned, and ask what else you could ask next time.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your message and your title.
Ask it: is my message clear and easy to understand?
Ask it to suggest one way to make my poster even better.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: from what I found, what is one good new question I could research?
Ask it to help me plan my very next research step.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fixed questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your new questions are fair now.
Ask it to show you one more way to fix any question you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it which answer was your strongest, and why.
Ask it to give you one more question like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask it which research skill to work on next, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask someone at home which topic they think is most important for children: keeping fit, healthy food, or screen-time.
Write down their answer.
Bring it, and your own ideas, to your next teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: Interview an elder at home
lines: With a grown-up's help, ask an older family member how children kept fit when they were young.
Use open questions that start with How or What.
Write their answers in your research book, and bring the best one to your teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: A real-world step
lines: With a grown-up's help, ask your questions to two or three family members or neighbours.
Write their answers in your research book.
Bring what you find to your next teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: Share it at home and at school
lines: Ask if your elder has a photo or a story from when they were young.
Write the most interesting thing you learned in your research book.
Bring it to your next teacher session to compare with other children.

toolkit.title: What is research?
toolkit.intro:
Research means finding out about a topic in a careful, organised way, so you can trust what you learn and share it with others. It is not just typing a question into a phone.

When you research, you really do three things: you ask good questions, you find useful sources to answer them, and you keep a record of what you find. Two habits help most. Use more than one source, because one source can be wrong. And write in your own words, because that is honest and clear.

toolkit.title: The steps of research
toolkit.intro: Whatever your topic, research follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Decide on a topic to find out about.
Make good questions.
Choose sources and make a questionnaire.
Ask people your questions.
Record your results in a chart or pictogram.
Check what your evidence shows.
Share your findings with a chart or a poster.

toolkit.title: Your research learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your research skills grow in three stages this year. Here are your goals for each stage, in simple words. It is fine to be working on any stage.

toolkit.title: Words to start a good question
toolkit.intro: Stuck for a question? These little words help you make one. Use them to start your questions.
items: What — What do children eat for lunch?
Where — Where do children like to play?
When — When do children do their sport?
Why — Why do some children do very little sport?
How — How can we help more children be active?
How many — How many children walk to school?

toolkit.title: Open questions and number questions
toolkit.intro: Two kinds of question help you in different ways. Good research uses some of each.

rows: It is answered in your own words.
What do you like to do after school?
It is answered with a number you can count.
How many days a week do you play sport?

toolkit.title: Ways to start a question for people
toolkit.intro:
When you ask people questions in a questionnaire or interview, these gentle starters work well. Keep them short and fair.

Try not to start with 'You agree that ...?' or 'Is it not true that ...?'. Those push people to one answer, and that is not fair.
items: How often do you ...?
How many ...?
What do you like about ...?
How do you feel about ...?
Can you tell me about ...? (great for an interview)

toolkit.title: Which source should I use?
toolkit.intro: Different questions need different sources. Pick the one that fits your question best.

rows: When you want facts others have found.
When you want to see how to do something.
How do I kick a football well?
When you want a real story or memory.
How did children play long ago?
When you want to find out about people near you.
How do children at my school keep fit?

toolkit.title: How to make a pictogram or chart
toolkit.intro:
A pictogram is a picture chart. Each small picture, or icon, stands for one thing, like one person. It makes your results easy to see.

A bar chart works in a similar way, using bars instead of pictures. The taller the bar, the more people chose that answer.
items: Choose a small picture to stand for one person.
Draw one picture for each person who gave that answer.
Add a key that says what one picture means.
Give your pictogram a clear title.

toolkit.title: How to make notes under headings
toolkit.intro: When you read a source, do not copy it. Make notes: short reminders in your own words. Keep them tidy by sorting them under headings.
items: Choose a few headings before you start, like Games, School, and Home.
Write short notes under each heading, in your own words.
It is fine if a heading has no notes. That source just did not tell you about it.
Write down which source each note came from.

toolkit.title: Ways to share your findings
toolkit.intro: When you have found something out, share it clearly so others understand. Pick the way that fits your findings best.
items: A pictogram or chart — great for numbers, like how many children play sport.
A poster — great for one strong message you want people to act on.
A short talk — tell your class or family what you found, in a few clear sentences.
A table — good for putting facts side by side to compare them.

toolkit.title: Staying safe and being fair
toolkit.intro: A good researcher is safe and kind. These habits are part of the skill, not extra rules.
items: Stay safe online. Never share your full name, address or school with strangers, and tell a trusted adult if a page worries you.
Be kind when you ask people. Say hello, say thank you, and let them choose not to answer.
Be fair. People see things in different ways. Listen to all of them before you make up your mind.
Only say what your evidence really shows. Do not say more than your results can prove.

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this a good question?
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, change your question.
items: Clear — it is easy to understand.
About my topic — it helps me find out what I want.
Fair — it does not push people to one answer.
Answerable — I can really find out the answer.

challenge.intro: Look back at the topic list in the Lesson file: keeping fit and healthy, how children spend their time, where our food comes from, or how children live in other countries. Choose one you care about, or think of your own.
topics: Write your topic in one sentence: 'My topic is ...'.
Write one reason you care about it.
Write one reason other people might care about it too.
checkpoints: I was surprised to find out that ...

activities.title: What do you already know?
activities.label: Activity 2: What do you already know?
activities.intro:
Before you research something new, it helps to think about what you already believe. Here are six ways children can make healthy choices. Put them in order, from 1 (most important) to 6 (least important), in your own opinion.

There is no single right answer here. This is your opinion. Write your number 1 choice, and one reason why you put it first.
steps: Eat fresh fruit and vegetables.
Play sport at least once a week.
Drink water instead of sugary drinks.
Spend time playing outdoors.
Have less time on phones and screens.
Get enough sleep at night.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your number 1 choice and your reason.
Ask it which choice it would put first, and why.
Ask it: is there a healthy choice not on the list that you would add?

activities.title: Make your own questions
activities.label: Activity 3: Make your own questions
activities.intro: Before you can research, you need questions. Make lots of them first. Use the little words What, Where, Why and How to help you.
steps: Write your topic in the middle of a page and draw a circle around it.
Around it, write at least six questions about your topic.
Try to use What, Where, Why and How to start your questions.
Put a star next to the two questions you most want to answer.

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Topic in the middle: keeping fit at my school.
Questions around it: What do children do at break? Why do some do little sport? How can we help more children be active? Where do children like to play?
These questions come from different angles, which is exactly what you want.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it which two questions look the most interesting, and why.
Ask it to suggest one good question you did not think of.

activities.title: Put the steps in order
activities.label: Activity 4: Put the steps in order
activities.intro:
An investigation works best in the right order. Below, the six steps are all mixed up. Write them out in the correct order, from first to last.

Write the six steps as a numbered list, 1 to 6, in the order you think is right.
steps: Ask some people your questions.
Tell others what you found out.
Decide on a topic to find out about.
Record your results.
Think of questions to ask.
Make a questionnaire.

boxes.title: Why the order matters
lines: You cannot make a questionnaire until you have thought of your questions first.
You cannot record results until you have asked people.
Telling others always comes last, because you need something to tell them.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your order to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check that your six steps are in the right order.
Ask it to explain any step you put in the wrong place.

activities.title: Make and run a mini questionnaire
activities.label: Activity 5: Make and run a mini questionnaire
activities.intro: Now gather your own information. This is the exciting part, because you find out something no book could tell you. Make a small questionnaire and ask a few people.
steps: Write three simple questions about your topic.
Make sure each one is easy to understand and quick to answer.
Decide who you will ask. Two or three children or family members is plenty.
Ask each person the same questions, and write down their answers.

boxes.title: A model questionnaire
lines: Topic: how children keep fit.
Question 1: How many days a week do you play sport or run around?
Question 2: What is your favourite way to be active?
Question 3: How many hours a day do you spend sitting still?
Notice there are number questions and open questions mixed together.

boxes.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It is short and easy to understand.
It is about your topic.
It can be answered quickly.
It does not push people to one answer. Ask 'How much sport do you do?', not 'You love sport, do you not?'.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a grown-up's help, ask your questions to two or three family members or neighbours.
Write their answers in your research book.
Bring what you find to your next teacher session.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are any of my questions hard to understand, or do any push people to one answer?
Ask it to help you fix any question that is not quite right.

activities.title: Make a pictogram of your results
activities.label: Activity 6: Make a pictogram of your results
activities.intro: A pictogram turns your answers into a picture chart. Each small picture stands for one person. It makes your results easy to see.
steps: Choose a small picture to stand for one person, like a stick figure.
For each answer, draw one picture. So if three children said sport, draw three figures.
Add a key that says: one picture means one child.
Give your pictogram a clear title.

boxes.title: A model pictogram
lines: Title: How my friends spend time after school.
Homework: four figures. Sport: two figures. Phone or computer: five figures.
Key: one figure means one child.
In one look, you can see which activity is the most popular.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what your pictogram shows.
Ask it: what is the clearest thing my pictogram tells us?
Ask it if my title makes it easy to understand.

activities.title: Match the question to the right source
activities.label: Activity 7: Match the question to the right source
activities.intro: Different questions need different sources. Match each question (1 to 4) to the source (A to D) most likely to answer it. Write the pairs, like 1-C.
steps: How do I get better at football?
What foods make a healthy lunch?
How did children play long ago?
What fun games can I play outside?
A. A recipe website about healthy meals.
B. A video that shows football skills.
C. A children's website about outdoor games.
D. An older family member who remembers the past.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four pairs to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check your matches.
Ask it: for my own Challenge, which kind of source would help me most?

activities.title: Sort open questions and number questions
activities.label: Activity 8: Sort open questions and number questions
activities.intro:
Remember, an open question is answered in your own words. A number question is answered with a number. Sort the six questions below. Write O for open, or N for number, next to each letter.

Then write one open question and one number question of your own about your topic.
steps: A. How many days a week do you play sport?
B. What do you like to do after school?
C. How many hours do you sleep at night?
D. Why do you enjoy that game?
E. How many cups of water do you drink each day?
F. How do you feel after playing outside?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any you found tricky.
Ask it: when is a number question more useful than an open question?

activities.title: Interview a family elder
activities.label: Activity 9: Interview a family elder
activities.intro: Older family members are wonderful sources. Interview one about how children kept fit and healthy when they were young. First plan your questions, then make notes under headings.
steps: Make a mind map: write 'keeping fit long ago' in the middle, and draw lines to things to ask about, like games, school, and food.
Write three open questions that start with How or What.
With a grown-up's help, ask an older family member your questions.
Make notes under headings: Ways they were active, Keeping fit at school, Keeping fit at home.

boxes.title: Being a kind interviewer
lines: Say hello and thank the person for helping you.
Ask one question at a time, and listen carefully.
It is fine to ask them to say more about an answer you like.
Never rush them. A good interview feels like a friendly chat.

boxes.title: Share it at home and at school
lines: Ask if your elder has a photo or a story from when they were young.
Write the most interesting thing you learned in your research book.
Bring it to your next teacher session to compare with other children.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three interview questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are my questions open, so they get long answers?
After the interview, tell it what you learned, and ask what else you could ask next time.

activities.title: Make a poster to persuade
activities.label: Activity 10: Make a poster to persuade
activities.intro: Findings are only useful if others understand them. Make a poster that shares your message and helps people change. Sana made a poster to persuade children to be more active. You can make one about your own Challenge.
steps: Write your one strong message in a sentence.
Think of a short, catchy title for the top.
Plan two or three pictures that help your message.
Make a first draft of your poster on a big sheet of paper.

boxes.title: A model poster plan
lines: Message: children should move more and play outside.
Title: Keep moving, keep healthy!
Pictures: children playing football, a child walking to school, a happy face.
One clear message, a big title, and pictures that help. That is a strong poster.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your message and your title.
Ask it: is my message clear and easy to understand?
Ask it to suggest one way to make my poster even better.

practice.intro: Answer these in your research book or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 14 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky. Try each one before you look at the answer key, and use your own words.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'research' mean?
practice.answer: Research means finding out about a topic in an organised way, so you can trust it and share it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Name two little words that help you make good questions.
practice.answer: Any two of: What, Where, Why, How.

practice.prompt: A sheet of questions you ask many people is called a ______.
practice.answer: A questionnaire.

practice.prompt: When you ask your questions to just one person, that is called an ______.
practice.answer: An interview.

practice.prompt: A picture chart, where one picture stands for one person, is called a ______.
practice.answer: A pictogram.

practice.prompt: True or false: 'How many days a week do you play sport?' is a number question.
practice.answer: True.

practice.prompt: An open question lets people answer in their own ______.
practice.answer: Words (their own words).

practice.prompt: Which source is best for 'How do I get better at football?': a recipe book, or a video that shows football skills?
practice.answer: A video that shows football skills.

practice.prompt: When you read a source, should you copy it, or make notes in your own words?
practice.answer: Make notes in your own words.

practice.prompt: A short title for a group of notes is called a ______.
practice.answer: A heading.

practice.prompt: Facts you have gathered, which show if something is true, are called ______.
practice.answer: Evidence.

practice.prompt: Name one good way to share your findings with other people.
practice.answer: Any one of: a pictogram, a chart, or a poster.

practice.prompt: A way of seeing something, or a point of view, is called a ______.
practice.answer: A perspective.

practice.prompt: If you only have one source, what is a good way to be more sure your answer is right?
practice.answer: Look at another source, to check the answer is the same. (Use more than one source.)

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each research word (1 to 6) to the right meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, like 1-C.
practice.prompt: Questionnaire
options: A. A picture chart where one picture stands for one person.
B. A sheet of questions you ask many people.
C. The facts you gather that show if something is true.
D. Anywhere your information comes from, like a book or a person.
E. Asking your questions to one person.
F. A way of seeing something; your point of view.
practice.answer: B — A sheet of questions you ask many people.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Interview
practice.answer: E — Asking your questions to one person.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Pictogram
practice.answer: A — A picture chart where one picture stands for one person.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Source
practice.answer: D — Anywhere your information comes from, like a book or a person.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Perspective
practice.answer: F — A way of seeing something; your point of view.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evidence
practice.answer: C — The facts you gather that show if something is true.

practice.intro: These short questions ask you to use what you learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Sana wants to know how much sport many children do. Should she use a questionnaire, or interview just one person? Why?
practice.answer: A questionnaire, because she wants answers from many children, not just one.

practice.prompt: Karim wants to know how his grandfather played long ago. Which source is best, and why?
practice.answer: His grandfather, because he remembers the past and no book knows his story.

practice.prompt: Nadia has a list of answers. What is a clear way to show them as a picture?
practice.answer: A pictogram, where one picture stands for one person.

practice.prompt: Omar reads that children do little sport. He wants to say children hate sport. Is that fair, if his results never asked about it?
practice.answer: No, it is not fair. His results never asked about liking sport, so the evidence does not show it.

practice.prompt: Leila found one website. What should she do to be more sure her answer is right?
practice.answer: Look at a second source, to check the answer is the same.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own speed ...
Working with my AI tutor, my partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking someone at home, like an older family member ...

vocabulary.meaning: The facts you gather that show whether something is true.
The things you find out from your research.
Facts and details about a topic.

A picture of your ideas, with your topic in the middle and lines to other ideas.
Questions people answer in their own words.
A question people answer with a number you can count.
What someone thinks or believes; others may not agree.
The answers and information you collect.
A way of seeing something; your point of view.
A picture chart where one picture stands for one thing, like one person.
A good guess about what you think you will find.
A sheet of questions you ask many people.
Anywhere your information comes from: a book, website, video or person.
A short title for a group of notes.
Short reminders of the important ideas, in your own words.
An important topic or problem that people want to find out about.
A picture that shows numbers or results, so they are easy to see.
To write down or save your results so you do not forget them.

I can put the steps of an investigation in order.
